ARCHITECTURAL DESIGN CHARACTERISTICS,
USES, AND PERCEPTIONS OF COMMUNITY
SPACES IN PERMANENT SUPPORTIVE HOUSING
YelenaMcLane,Ph.D. andJillPable,Ph.D.,FloridaStateUniversity,USA
ABSTRACT
People experiencing homelessness often face recoveries complicated by mental disability, sub-
stance abuse, and trauma. They can withdraw into self-imposed isolation and avoid important
support services, making recovery more difficult. Affirmative relationships developed in part
within the designed settings of transitional housing may play a significant role in countering
these tendencies. The presence and effectiveness of communal gathering spaces in supportive
housing must be better understood as a design problem, particularly given users’ diverse ages,
ethnicities, and health needs, which effectively inclusive environments must accommodate. In
recent decades, architecture as a discipline has pivoted toward more human-centered
approaches, with the individual’sdignity and well-being at center stage. This study applies social
science-based research methods and spatial analytics to the end of understanding how specific
interior spaces, key to the recovery process, might be improved. The authors posit that the suc-
cess of resident gathering spaces intended to prompt and support resident relationships and
decrease users’ feelings of marginalization may be influenced by a range of sociospatial design
factors (i.e. visibility and ease of access, adjacencies, access to daylight and views, furniture
types, and aesthetics) together with facility policies and events programming. The authors use a
combination of space syntax, surveys, and qualitative methods to analyze two contrasting lay-
outsinsupportivehousing locationsintheUKandFlorida,drawingconclusionsintendedtosteer
thedevelopmentoftypologiesforsimilarfacilities.
INTRODUCTION
In Address Unknown: The Homeless in America (2009), James D. Wright wrote that “aside from
the absence of stable housing, there is no single characteristic that all homeless people share:
some are old men, some are young women, and some are infants and children” (p. 55). People
become homeless for a range of reasons—loss of a job; loss of a wage-earning family member;
loss of housing due to a natural disaster or fire; or loss of personal income and stability as the
resultofdomesticviolence,substanceabuse,orphysicalormentalillness(Cancaro, 2013).
In recent years, as economic resources and the social safety net have shrunk, the number of
homeless persons has risen (Bloomfield, 2013). Persons most at risk of entering homelessness
are those who grew up in poverty, with unsupportive families, and with few or no educational
opportunities or financial resources. Some have repeatedly experienced early childhood, adoles-
cent, or adult trauma; physical, psychological, or emotional abuse; or domestic violence. They
may be mentally ill or addicted to alcohol or drugs. They may have served time in juvenile
detention homes, jails, or prisons, and they often have little or no access to medical, dental, or
mental health services (ibid). In the United States, one third of the homeless are military
veterans.
Among homeless persons, there are much greater incidences of a range of health problems

HOMELESSNESS AND THE PHYSICAL ENVIRONMENT
The World Health Organization defines health broadly as a “state of complete physical, mental
and social well-being” and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity (World Health Organi-
zation, 1946:2018). Within the context of persons experiencing homelessness, aspects of a
healthy life include: healthy environments (buildings and immediate surroundings both indoors
and out of doors); positive relationships and mutual respect among and between service users,
volunteers, and staff; opportunities for meaningful occupations; and health-related activities to
addresssmoking,obesity,andsubstance misuse.
Homelessness israrelyexploredfromthe point ofview ofindividuals’ relationships totheir physi-
calsurroundings,which playa significantroleinmanagingtraumarecovery and inself-perception
and self-actualization as worthy members of society (Hopper, Bassuk, & Olivet, 2009; Pannell,
2007; Rivlin & Moore, 2001). To understand and help persons experiencing homelessness, their
needs must be at the center of both social policies and design solutions (Henwood, Cabassa,
Craig,&Padgett,2013;Hopperetal.,2009;Pannell,2007;Rivlin&Moore,2001).Thearchitecture
and interior design of permanent supportive housing can help to create environments in which
affirmativerelationshipscandevelop(Huffman,2018;Pannell,2007;Rivlin&Moore,2001).

through the 2009 $1.5 billion American Recovery and Reinvestment Act federal fund (111th
United States Congress, 2009). It is now supported by the Department of Housing and Urban
Development and endorsed by the United States Interagency Council on Homelessness (United
States Interagency Council on Homelessness, 2015). More than 30 cities and states have
adopted this approach, in addition to countries including Finland, Australia, Sweden, and Japan
(Australian Housing anf Urban Research Institute, 2018; Housing Futures, 2018; Médecins du
mondeJapan,2017;SchoolofSocialWork,2019).
Despite the growing acceptance of the Housing First model, which requires on-site support,
detailed analysis of the architectural design of supportive housing has received little attention.
Exploration of discrete architectural environments may be the next step as current literature
offers onlybroad conclusions. In her 2007 study of hostel culture and how to improve the health
and well-being of homeless and other vulnerable people, Jenny Pannell posited that buildings in
poor condition convey negative messages to “service users” (i.e. residents) and staff and that
“better buildings can facilitate new ways of working and make both service users and staff feel
valued” (Pannell, 2007, p. 7). Current studies that query residents about their experience of sup-
portive housing have similarly treated the idea of home very generally, without exploring specific
experiencesoflivinginsuchplaces.Studieshaveaskedformerlyhomelessresidentsiftheirhomes
offered them a “good environment” (Palepu, Hubley, Russell, Gadermann & Chinni, 2012; Tsai,
Mares & Rosenheck, 2012) or were “in good repair” (O’Connell, Rosenheck, Kasprow & Frisman,
2006). There is, however, very little known about residents’ feelings, perceptions, or emotional
connectionstothedesignaspectsofsupportspacesinpermanenthousing.
Social assistance helps significantly with the process of exiting homelessness (Rivlin & Moore,
2001) and therefore serves as a suitable goal for built environment support. Maintaining con-
tactswithfriends,clinicalstaff,andfamilymembersmayleadtoresourcesincludingfood,cloth-
ing, and emotional support. Social assistance exists in part to counter the marginalized
individual’s tendency to go through self-imposed isolation—a serious problem for persons
experiencing homelessness and its related issues—as withdrawal is related to depression, a
senseofhelplessnessandhopelessness,andprematuredeath(AmericanCancer Society,2018).

It logically follows that the presence and effectiveness of communal gathering spaces in sup-
portive housing is important, particularly as a hedge against the downward spiral of isolation
(M. Smith, personal communication, May 14, 2018). Such spaces are intended to impart a sense
of community so that a person may be reintroduced to the process of building productive rela-
tionships. This sensitivity to socialization goals is also reflected in a recent paradigm change in
support strategies emanating from the psychology and social work fields, placing at the center
thedignityandwell-beingofserviceusers.
TRAUMA-INFORMED CARE
Some architects and designers are adopting new approaches to facilities for persons experienc-
ing homelessness consistent with the tenets of trauma-informed care (TIC). TIC acknowledges
that the effects of strife and adversity in a person’s life significantly shape their perceptions and
actions concerning homelessness and its attendant issues. It rejects top–down, authoritarian
approaches to social support and reemphasizes physical, psychological, and emotional safety. It
advocates expanding opportunities for residents to access peer support and collaborate with
staff members on trauma management strategies with the goal of increasing control over their
lives. TIC promotes personal empowerment, voice, and choice (Hopper et al., 2009; Substance
Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, 20141). Built environments guided by TIC
principles or, as some have termed it, “trauma-informed design” (Committee on Temporary
Shelter, n.d.) allow residents to build resilience and recover their positive sense of self as a
means to re-enter society as healthy and productive individuals. Designers should understand

study of a permanent supportive housing project, Huffman (2018) has argued that TIC and
design allow organizations to provide contexts for human thriving that go beyond training staff
and designing for services (which may include supervision, consultation, and assessment) to cre-
ate comprehensive services informed by customer input (see also Hopper et al., 2009). Huffman
emphasizes that built environments can and should be a component of the treatment experi-
encebecauseenvironmentscarrywiththemassociations thatmightbeharnessedforhealing.
Although research has addressed the importance of relationships to building a sense of connec-
tion and avoiding self-imposed isolation (Alcaraz et al., 2019; Holt-Lunstad, Smith, Baker, Har-
ris, & Stephenson, 2015), studies that examine the potential of actual gathering spaces within
sheltersorsupportivehousingsituationstocombatself-isolationarefew.Huffman(2018)exam-
ined resident attitudes concerning key social spaces—a community garden, kitchen, and TV
room—managed by The Skid Row Housing Trust within the Star Apartments in Los Angeles. His
findings indicate that, although the trauma-informed design of community spaces in permanent
supportive housing can support well-being and recovery by facilitating encounters and interac-
tions, other factors such as involvement with social activities and policies and rules (that influ-
enceaccessandusefairness)wereoftendispositive ofresidents’perceptionsofthefacility.
A small group of studies has focused on how built environments may improve users’ well-being
by supporting interpersonal interaction and socialization. A study of student resident housing
conducted by Kader, Zhiri, Bucher, Spreckelmeyer, and Tipton (2017) identified that design fea-
tures such as location of social spaces, furniture layout, aesthetics (color and light), and the

pus student life centers, McLane and Kozinets (2019) found that easily accessible location and
prominent visual presence of social spaces, ambiguous space programming, and users’ control
over activities within and navigation through spaces facilitate the use of social spaces. Yang and
Stark (2010) explored similar factors in an assisted living facility, where residents stressed the
importance of accessible private and community spaces that allow for small social gatherings.
Social spaces close to other public functional spaces such as entrances, mailrooms, or laundry

RESEARCH QUESTIONS
This study examines the therapeutic role of community gathering spaces for single male and
female adults recovering from homelessness in permanent supportive housing situations and
aimstoaddressthefollowing threeresearch questions:
1. Are community spaces important for permanent supportive housing residents recover-
ingfromhomelessness?
2. What role do community spaces play in these residents’ formal and informal social
gatherings?
3. What sociospatial and design factors affect the desirability and use of community
spaces?
In keeping with the literature discussed above, the authors posit that the success of resident
gathering spaces may be influenced by a range of sociospatial design factors (i.e. visibility and
ease of access, adjacencies, access to daylight and views, furniture types and layout, and aes-
thetics)togetherwithfacilitypoliciesandeventsprogramming.
METHODS AND ANALYSIS
This dual case study embraced a mixed-method approach in data gathering and analysis. It
examinedtheperceptionsofresidentsandemployeesoflocation,design,anduseofcommunity
spaces in two permanent supportive housing locations—one in Southampton, UK, and one in
Tallahassee, Florida—with the intent to draw conclusions that may inform future decision-
makingforsimilarfacilities.
The exploratory nature and questions of the inquiry determined the primarily qualitative nature
of the study. A case study design allows for examining a phenomenon up close, indepth, and in
its natural context (Yin, 2018). Cases are not read as isolated experiences or events but are
reflective of the broad and dynamic settings in which the data are gathered, where relevant
information may come from multiple sources (Yin, 2012). As Eisner (1998) has observed, human
experience is qualitative in nature, and it would be only logical to apply our analytical tools in
innovativewaystoidentifyandtracepatternsofourbehavior,socialstructures,andculture.
The researchers used several data collection methods over a 12-week study period: open-ended
interviews, exploratory questionnaires, space syntax analytical tools, and photography. As noted
in the literature review, the number of studies that investigated how persons who have experi-
enced homelessness responded to their built environment is limited. This prompted the authors
to develop new interview and questionnaire instruments based on relevant literature; their
experiences working on related subjects, population groups (e.g. Pable, 2007, 2012), and meth-
odology (McLane, 2014:2019); and research questions. The questions were tested and discussed

1. Exploratory questionnaires contained 27 questions (including multiple choice, Likert

ticipant preferences in using these spaces. The participants were recruited through
posted fliers (residents and staff) and via email communication (staff). Select persons
who indicated their willingness to continue their participation were then invited for
follow-up interviews. The quantitative questionnaire data were analyzed using descrip-

2. Open-ended interviews with residents (in-person) and staff (in-person and one via
Skype) lasted on average about 40minutes. The questions (25 total) asked the partici-
pants to expand on their questionnaire answers and engage interviewees in in-depth
conversations yielding rich descriptions and mini-narratives that brought valuable
insights to the data. Interviews with staff provided relevant information about the
sites’ policies and rules for residents. The interviews were voice recorded, transcribed,
andcodedusingDedoose.3
There was a total of 38 respondents between the two locations: 28 survey participants
(both residents and staff) and 18 interviewees (see Table 1). The disproportionate
number of participants between the twostudy locations reflects challenges insoliciting
participation from residents (particularly in the overseas location) who may have lim-
ited access to computers and may not be open to sharing their thoughts and experi-
ences online. This resulted in the Booth Centre resident data coming primarily from
interviews,whiletheWestgatelocationyieldedbothsurveysandinterviews.
3. The data for space syntax analysis4 came from the sites’ floor plans, which were
convertedintovisibilitygraphsgeneratedbydepthmapX.5
4. Photography was used to document the community spaces and their uses in both
locations.
Data triangulation strengthened the reliability of this study. The four datasets were analyzed
and superimposed, allowing for a robust substantiation and corroboration of findings within
each set. An interview sample of ten residents (five in each location) and 12 staff (nine in the
Booth Centre and all three staff in the Westgate Community) allowed information to be cross-
checkedandamorecompleteunderstandingofthephenomenaunderinvestigation toemerge.
LOCATIONS
The two case studies selected for this inquiry represent two typical permanent supportive hous-
ing approaches: first, they house an existing assistance program and therefore reflect today’s
social/charitable support practices; second, they occupy existing (although modified to different
degrees) buildings; and third, they feature two different floor layout options (discussed in
greaterdetailbelow).

arranged in a cluster configuration within a four-story building. The client population has

ASSUMPTIONS, LIMITATIONS, AND DELIMITATIONS
The literature review for this study provided a basis for the researchers’ assumption that social
connections and support play an important role in helping persons exit homelessness and
recover from illnesses, stresses, and hardships that often accompany this condition. Built envi-
ronments can assist inthis process by providingcommunity spaces in which supportive relation-
ships may develop. It is important to recognize, however, that not all persons who have
experienced homelessness are able to establish or maintain social relationships or feel that they
needsocialsupport,thusdismissingtheperceivedneedforcommunityspacesamongresidents.
Asmentionedinthe methodology section, accessing and working directlywith persons who had
experienced homelessness was a challenge. Despite careful precautions and assurances of ano-
nymity and nondisclosure the researchers gave to residents, participants may have believe that
the facility administration was aware of their participation. This may have affected their
responses (i.e. prompting more complimentary answers about the facilities’ designs and poli-
cies). The researchers also observed that a number of resident participants spoke in dry, institu-
tionalized language of personal responsibility and asserted that they were grateful for even
being in this facility. In this situation, the researchers took extra efforts to triangulate the data
by obtaining in-depth descriptions from other resident participants and staff by using multiple
methodsofinformationcollectionandanalysis.
Thequestionnairesample size presents a limitation for generalizing the findings derived from its
data alone. In this study, the quantitative questionnaires were important but secondary instru-
ments serving as points of entry into the larger inquiry. The overall goal was to record and
explore a phenomenon of community spaces in permanent supportive housing, their architec-
tural qualities, and investigate how and why residents engage (or do not engage) with these
JOURNALOFINTERIORDESIGN 39

spaces. This approach did not result in empirically verifiable results generalizable to a broader
population. Rather, the researchers sought to offer a compelling picture and present new ways
of analyzing the complexity of the relationships between built environments, social spaces, and
personswhohaveexperiencedhomelessness.
The study did not address any background characteristics of the respondents, such as personal
histories, relationships, health, or where they were in the process of exiting homelessness with
regard to residents or the hierarchy of organization, experience with working with homeless
persons,orposition(i.e.caseworkerormanagement)withregardtostaff.
RESULTS
IMPORTANCE OF HAVING COMMUNITY SPACES AND A SENSE OF COMMUNITY
Staff in both locations observed that it is very important for residents to have a sense of com-
munity. Case managers from the Booth Centre observed how their residents often come in for
initial interviews feeling unimportant, anxious, or that their lives lack meaning. The transition
from the street into housing is a stressful process, which may lead to isolation and sometimes
endsinsuicide.Itis,therefore,veryimportanttohelpresidentstofeelsupportedthroughinter-
actionsandsocialization,tohelpthemtounderstandthatthey“meansomethingintheworld.”
The first research question addressed whether participants perceived community spaces to be
important to them personally. The results from the two sites largely coincided. The majority of
resident and all staff participants in the two study locations indicated that it was important to
havecommunity spacesinthe facility.Thesummaryofthese resultsisgiven inTable2.ABooth
Centre resident remarked that, “it is good to have acquaintances and friends you can trust. It is
startingtohelpmeopenupbecauseI’mshyandstepoutofmycomfortzone.”AWestgateres-
ident noted that being able to come to community spaces and socialize (whether by just seeing
other people, talking to others, or participating in activities) is even more important for resi-
dents with mental issues who might especially benefit from getting out of their room and being
distracted from their recurring thoughts or compulsive activities. Another Booth Centre inter-
vieweefurthersuggestedthatbeingabletosocialize“isahumanrightsissue.”
COMMUNITY SPACES ARE UNDERUSED WHILE SERVING AS SOCIAL SPACES FOR MANY
ACTIVITIES
The second question concerned the role of community spaces in residents’ formal and informal
social gatherings. Staff and resident survey and interview data suggest that community spaces
are typically used by only one person or small groups of two or three persons at a time. Situa-
tions in which there are larger user groups are rare. The degree of use varied between the two
sites. Over 90% of Westgate resident participants use the community spaces regularly, and 86%
reported using them twice a week or more. None of the Booth Centre participants reported
usingtheloungespaceintheirbuilding.
The staff organizes or helps to hold a limited number of planned activities in the community
spaces in both locations. Data from Westgate showed that only 6% of participants reported
attending such events during their residence. The majority of informal activities in the

Although the majority of the study participants (both survey and interviews) agreed on the ben-
efits of socialization and need to form a community of residents, in-depth conversations with
residents and staff indicated that the community spaces in both facilities do not get much use.
Anecdotal evidence collected for this study may suggest a possible explanation for this seeming
contradiction. As human beings, we have an innate need to socialize and realize its importance
for our well-being. Psychological states of the residents (many of whom are still experiencing
high levels of trauma and stress associated with “sleeping rough” or transitioning into new
places where they feeluncomfortable) or mental health conditions may preclude residents from
seeking out opportunities for socializing. Two resident participants (one in each location)
suggested that residents who do not use the community spaces may have more highly
introverted personality types or suffer from depression or other mental disabilities. These data,
although interesting, warrant further investigation apart from this study. The second factor is
real or perceived antisocial (aggressive, unwelcoming, bullying) behaviors by other residents.
While antisocial behaviors appear to influence the use of community spaces, this too lies
beyondthescopeofthisstudy.
SPATIAL FACTORS AND DESIRABILITY OF COMMUNITY SPACES
The third research question focused on sociospatial and design factors that affect the desirabil-
ity and use of community spaces in permanent supportive housing. Analysis of spatial
layouts, individual and social activities data, and organizations’ stated policies indicated three
categories of factors that influence use: (1) spatial design, (2) aesthetics, and (3) institutional
policies.6
Bysuperimposingquestionnaireandinterviewdatawithspatialanalysis,theresearchersidentified
several spatial design factors that influenced the nature and frequency of usage of resident com-
munityspaces.Indescendingorderofreportedfrequency,theseare:locationinthebuilding,visi-
bilityintoandfromthespace,wayfinding,size,andadjacenciestokitchensandprivaterooms.
On these points, the two locations differed somewhat. Westgate’s community spaces are at the
front of several identical standalone houses, making them easily accessible to residents upon
entering the building. This is a large space divided in half by a major pathway along the build-
ing’s longitudinal axis (Figures 2 and 3). Most rooms are furnished with a sofa, an arm chair,
perhaps additional side chairs, and a television set. Staff and resident participants found that
the lounges are adequate in size and in quality of lighting, with furniture meeting some or most
(although basic) user needs. The majority of participants perceived the space as easy to see and
access, adequately sized, well lit, and found that the furniture met most of their needs. Despite
these positive perceptions, few residents actually used the space, with only a handful of resi-
dents reporting having cooked in the kitchen. A few residents bring their food from elsewhere
and eat at a large community table, which they also use for writing, to do crossword puzzles, or

Spacesyntax analytical methods areusefulfordetermininghowlayouts function, demonstrating

JUSTIFIEDGRAPHS
Justified graphs represent spatial relationships between adjacent spaces and identify direct
connections (also defined as syntactic steps) between those spaces (Hillier & Hanson, 1997)
(Figure 5). Entrance points are depicted as root spaces at the bottom of the diagrams. All
spaces connected to the root space are one syntactic step away and are drawn one level
up. The more levels the justified graph has, the deeper and less accessible the space may be
for users. Spatial relationships represented by justified graphs may form branching struc-

SUMMARY OF FINDINGS
Although the two locations’ configurations could not be more different, the researchers’ exami-
nation of spatial data and participant responses allowed for a determination that the lower-
than-expected use of community spaces in both locations may be influenced by three groups of
factors: spatial, aesthetic, and institutional policies. These observations are summarized here
withdesignsuggestions,furtherinformedbyliteraturereviewwhereapplicable.

Biographies
Yelena McLane is an assistant professor in the Interior Architecture & Design Department at
Florida State University. Her research interests lie in the spatial analysis of complex building sys-
tems. She explores relationships between interior configurations and users’ perceptions and
experiences within spaces, and institutional, social, and cultural influences upon these relation-
ships,tobetterinforminteriorarchitectureanddesignpractice.
JillPable isaprofessorintheInterior Architecture&DesignDepartment atFlorida State Univer-
sity. She holds degrees in Interior Design and a Ph.D. in Instructional Technology and is a fellow
oftheInteriorDesignEducatorsCouncilandisanNCIDQ-certifiedandaWELL-accreditedprofes-
sional. She facilitates Design Resources for Homelessness, a nonprofit knowledge resource that
hasbeenfeaturedinFastCompanyandNPR’sWeekendEdition.
